approach: Write the force needed to push the block up the incline and the force needed to barely hold it from sliding down, then use the given ratio between them.

steps.text: To push the block up, gravity's pull down the incline and friction (which now opposes the upward push) both work against the applied force.
To barely stop the block sliding down, friction acts up the incline at its full value and helps hold the block, so the needed applied force is smaller.
Use the given condition that F_up is twice F_hold, then divide through by mg cosθ and solve for tanθ.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving friction out of F_hold, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ + μcosθ = 2sinθ, so tanθ = μ.
Leaving friction out of F_up, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ = 2(sinθ − μcosθ), so tanθ = 2μ.
